description: Building an AI-assisted dashboard for detecting and explaining long-term Earth system trends with NASA data. Focus on clear visualizations, statistical significance, and practical insights. Solo for now, open to strong collaborators.
summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web application built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It turns raw NASA Earth-observation data into clear, defensible insights about how our planet is changing. A user picks an environmental variable, a geographic region, and a historical period. The app then pulls the matching NASA data and builds a time series. It runs statistical tests to check whether any trend is significant or just noise, and finally generates an investigation report that explains the findings.
The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind. Recharts handles the data visualisations, Framer Motion handles animation, and React Three Fiber provides an interactive 3D globe. The backend is a Python 3.11+ FastAPI service that uses Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and Statsmodels for the analysis. The frontend and backend is deployed on Vercel.
The goal is to make climate and Earth-system analysis accessible. Students, researchers, and curious citizens can explore real data and see statistically grounded conclusions without writing code.
details:
This application uses decades of NASA Earth science data to investigate trends in the Earth system. Click on a point on the 3D globe, search for a location or select a one-click hotspot, including the Arctic, Amazon, Sahel and Delhi. Choose from 8 different variables to investigate: skin temp, dew point, precipitation, root zone soil moisture, snow cover, specific humidity, aerosol optical depth & clear sky solar irradiance. The FastAPI backend pulls yearly and monthly data from NASA POWER (MERRA-2 reanalysis), removes seasonality and analyses for trends using the Hamed-Rao modified Mann-Kendall method. The magnitude of the trend is found using the Theil-Sen slope and OLS slope with 95% confidence intervals. Change points are identified using the Pettitt method. The report includes significant years, extreme years and a quality score for each time series. Comparison between locations and correlation between variables can also be carried out. The research assistant will answer questions using statistics that can be recalculated by the backend.

Benefits/Impact

Provides students/researchers with a thorough analysis without needing to write any code. Ultimately, the aim is for the general public to become aware of the impact we are having on our shared planet’s climate. Limitations are clearly stated. Significant results are not shown as proof of causation, and non-significant results are not shown as proof of no change.

Technologies

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Framer Motion, React Three Fibre

Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Statsmodels

Data: NASA POWER API (MERRA-2), AI Assistant (Google Gemini)

Hosting: Vercel. No special hardware used.

Creativity

The application acts like an investigator to answer questions. The evidence to back up the claim is shown and the limitations of the numbers are explained. The interactive 3D Earth Globe makes serious science fun.

As this was a single developer project, I focused on producing statistics that were honest. This included correctly accounting for missing data, serial correlation and known breaks in the source. Data quality badges were added to the project and the AI was protected from making up numbers. Automated testing was created and the code was structured with modularity in mind.
